clue.text: Grand in cash, say, for mischievous child

indicators.note: one thing being in another means it sits inside it

blocks.note: cash is one example of money, which the 'say' flags
a grand is a thousand, and K stands for thousand

explanation.surface: Someone asks what a thousand pounds in banknotes might buy for a naughty youngster.
explanation.walkthrough: K for a thousand slips inside MONEY. A monkey is also British slang for £500, a tempting but wrong double-definition reading of 'grand'.
explanation.definitionFit: Monkey is an affectionate everyday word for a cheeky, playful youngster who gets into trouble.

clue.text: Horse starts to amble into northern part of range

indicators.note: the starts of words are their opening letters
leading into the next item means coming straight before it in the line

blocks.note: a mount is a horse for riding
first letters of the two words
N is the abbreviation for northern

explanation.surface: A horse ambles up into the northern reaches of a mountain range.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Range' looks like open pasture for a horse, but here it is a mountain range.
explanation.definitionFit: A mountain range is a chain of peaks, so each single peak is one member of that chain.

clue.text: Trainee accountant discontentedly checking suspect invoice

indicators.note: without its contents a word keeps only its outer shell of letters
to check something is to hold it back, so one piece is held within another
something suspect is dodgy and not as it should be, so its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A junior accountant, unhappy at work, goes through a dodgy bill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trainee accountant' reads as one phrase, but the definition is just 'Trainee'; the accountant only supplies its two outer letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A noviciate, a variant of novitiate, is a novice or probationer still learning the ropes before full admission.

clue.text: Portray nude on a grand scale

indicators.note: a nude figure has been stripped of its outer covering, so the outside letters go

explanation.surface: An artist is told to paint a nude on a huge canvas.
explanation.walkthrough: Stripping DEPICT of its first and last letters leaves EPIC.
explanation.definitionFit: Epic describes anything vast and heroic in scope, the adjective matching that adverbial phrase about size.

clue.text: Part of book principal reportedly proscribed

indicators.note: what is reported is heard rather than seen, so the sound matters, not the spelling

blocks.note: a school principal is its head

explanation.surface: A headteacher has, it is said, banned a particular chapter of a book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Part of book' looks like the start of the wordplay, but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: In bookbinding a headband is the decorative strip of cloth at the top of the spine of a volume.

clue.text: English erected sign incorporating extremely refined circles

indicators.note: in a down clue, putting something up turns it bottom to top
the extremes of a word are its first and last letters
to incorporate is to take into the body, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: E is the abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: An English road sign has been put up with some elegant circular markings on it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Circles' looks like a noun for the markings, but it is a verb: surrounds.
explanation.definitionFit: To engird is to encircle or surround something, so engirds is the verb form of circles.

clue.text: Diabolic comedian fluffed a line

indicators.note: a performer who fluffs words garbles them, so the letters come out jumbled

blocks.note: L is the abbreviation for line

explanation.surface: A dreadful comic forgot a line on stage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Diabolic' looks like a verdict on the performance, but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Demoniacal means devilish or fiendish, a direct synonym for diabolic, both describing something like a demon.

clue.text: Assert old medical condition limits resistance

indicators.note: limits form a boundary, so one piece is bounded on both sides by another

blocks.note: ague is an old name for a malarial fever
R is the symbol for electrical resistance

explanation.surface: A claim that an old illness restricts a patient's ability to fight back.
explanation.walkthrough: AGUE holds R after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To argue a point is to maintain or contend that it is true, so both verbs mean put forward a claim.

clue.text: Old money essentially funding upper-class jazzmen

indicators.note: the essence of something is its core, so the central letter is kept

blocks.note: U is the standard abbreviation for upper-class
cats is slang for jazz musicians

explanation.surface: Inherited wealth is quietly bankrolling posh jazz players.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old money' suggests aristocratic wealth, but it is the definition: a former coin.
explanation.definitionFit: Ducats were gold and silver coins used across Europe for centuries, so they are currency from the past.

clue.text: Shame to keep case of Glenfarclas in farm outbuilding

indicators.note: a case is the outer shell, so only the outermost letters are kept
keeping something means holding it, so one piece is held inside another

blocks.note: as in 'it's a shame', 'it's a pity'
first and last letters; Glenfarclas is a Scotch whisky

explanation.surface: A pity to hide a case of fine whisky away in a farm shed.
explanation.walkthrough: PITY holds GS in its middle. Glenfarclas is a Speyside single malt.
explanation.definitionFit: A pigsty is the pen and shelter on a farm where pigs are housed, a small agricultural building.

clue.text: Terribly evil nun excited about one German's revelation

indicators.note: something done terribly is botched, so the letters are scrambled
excited things are stirred up, so these letters are mixed too
to be about something is to go around it

blocks.note: G is the abbreviation for German

explanation.surface: A wicked, agitated nun waits for a German to reveal something.
explanation.walkthrough: Two separate anagrams are at work here, each indicator rearranging just the word beside it, and the wimple-wearing nun neatly yields a veil.
explanation.definitionFit: An unveiling is a disclosure or reveal of something previously hidden, the same noun sense as revelation.

clue.text: Yours truly featured in publication about dark arts

indicators.note: what features in something appears within it

blocks.note: C is circa, Latin for about

explanation.surface: The setter boasts of appearing in a magazine article on witchcraft.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' looks like a link to the topic, but it is C, circa; I goes inside MAG + C.
explanation.definitionFit: Black magic and sorcery are the dark arts, so magic is the umbrella word for those occult practices.

clue.text: Some devout Catholics backed diplomacy

indicators.note: some of a phrase is only a part of its run of letters
going back means reading from right to left

blocks.note: a run spanning the two words

explanation.surface: A group of pious Catholics supported a diplomatic approach.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backed' reads as supported, but it signals reading the hidden letters in reverse.
explanation.definitionFit: Tact is sensitivity and skill in handling people delicately, which is the essence of diplomacy.

clue.text: Bitter struggle to take out a cracking spy

indicators.note: taking something out removes it
something cracking a shell breaks into it, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: a spy is a secret agent

explanation.surface: A bitter fight to assassinate a spy who has broken a case.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take out' sounds like killing, but it simply removes the letter A from the struggle word.
explanation.definitionFit: Astringent remarks are sharp and harsh, so the word works as a synonym for biting or bitter.

clue.text: Detective left picture taken after Greek expedition

indicators.note: coming after something places it later in the line

blocks.note: a PI is a private investigator
L is the abbreviation for left
GR is the abbreviation for Greek

explanation.surface: A sleuth leaves behind a photograph snapped after a trip to Greece.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left' looks like a verb, departed, but is just L.
explanation.definitionFit: A pilgrimage is a journey undertaken to a sacred place, a particular kind of long trip or expedition.

clue.text: Madness appearing without Suggs's ultimate folly

indicators.note: the ultimate item is the last one, so a final letter is taken
being without something means lacking it, so it is removed

explanation.surface: The pop band Madness playing without their frontman Suggs would be foolish.
explanation.walkthrough: Suggs is the lead singer of the British ska band Madness, which makes 'Madness' look like a proper noun. Dropping S from INSANITY gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Inanity is silliness or lack of sense, and folly likewise means foolish behaviour, so the nouns match.

clue.text: Famous actors catching international flight?

indicators.note: to catch something is to hold it inside

blocks.note: I is the abbreviation for international

explanation.surface: Celebrities hurrying to board an overseas plane.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flight' with 'international' suggests air travel; the question mark warns it is a flight of steps.
explanation.definitionFit: A flight is a series of steps between floors, which is what a set of stairs is.

clue.text: Ran through part of funeral cortège wearing scarlet

indicators.note: something worn is inside the clothing that covers it

blocks.note: scarlet is a shade of red
a hearse leads a funeral procession

explanation.surface: Someone dashed through a funeral procession dressed in bright red.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ran through' suggests running past or stabbing, but it means practised.
explanation.definitionFit: To run through a play or speech is to practise it beforehand, which is exactly what rehearsing means.

clue.text: Dunces love interrupting senior examiner

indicators.note: to interrupt is to break in, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: SR is the abbreviation for senior
love is zero in tennis scoring

explanation.surface: Romance between dimwitted pupils disrupts a senior examiner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Senior examiner' reads as one title, but 'senior' is SR, broken by O.
explanation.definitionFit: An assessor is a person who evaluates or grades work, the job an examiner does in a test.

clue.text: Significance of pause in speech

indicators.note: in speech words are heard, so sound counts, not spelling

explanation.surface: A speaker's dramatic pause adds meaning to what is said.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pause in speech' reads like an orator's technique, but 'in speech' signals the sound-alike.
explanation.definitionFit: Weight means importance or influence, as in giving weight to an argument, so it matches significance.

clue.text: Capture entertaining ace sporting bun

indicators.note: sporting can mean playful, and playing with letters jumbles them
to entertain guests is to have them inside, so one piece holds another

explanation.surface: A champion player wearing a bun is caught on camera.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sporting' looks like wearing, but it signals rearranging the ace before it goes inside, just after the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A teacake is a light sweet yeast bun, often with currants, usually toasted and buttered in Britain.

clue.text: Pains after exercise? Fruit is the answer!

indicators.note: coming after something places it later in the line

explanation.surface: Sore after a workout? Eating fruit will cure it.
explanation.walkthrough: PE is physical education, the school name for exercise classes.
explanation.definitionFit: Peaches are soft, sweet stone fruits with fuzzy skin, so they are an instance of the broader category.

clue.text: Swift pint at end of esplanade

indicators.note: sitting at the end of something places it last in the line

blocks.note: a prom is a seaside promenade
PT is the abbreviation for pint

explanation.surface: A quick beer at the end of a seafront walk.
explanation.walkthrough: An esplanade is a British seaside promenade, shortened to prom.
explanation.definitionFit: Prompt means done without delay, which matches swift as an adjective for quick action.

clue.text: Extinguish national spirit

blocks.note: first meaning: to put an end to, as with a rumour

explanation.walkthrough: 'National spirit' looks like patriotic feeling, but it is the drink Scotland is famous for.
explanation.definitionFit: To scotch a rumour is to quash it, and Scotch whisky is the spirit identified with one particular nation.

clue.text: Fierce critic got a racist sacked

indicators.note: a sacked place is ransacked and thrown into disorder

explanation.surface: An outspoken critic managed to get a bigot fired.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sacked' reads as dismissed from a job, but it signals scrambling.
explanation.definitionFit: To castigate is to rebuke severely, so a castigator is someone who harshly reprimands or condemns.

clue.text: Light-brown sweets son brought in for Charlie

indicators.note: bringing one player in for another means one replaces the other

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for son
Charlie is C in the NATO alphabet

explanation.surface: A boy fetches some toffee-coloured sweets for Charlie.
explanation.walkthrough: S replaces the C of CANDY.
explanation.definitionFit: Sandy describes a pale yellowish-brown colour like sand, commonly used of hair, so it matches the adjective.

clue.text: Degenerate artist meets knave on vacation

indicators.note: a vacated place is emptied, so only the outer letters are left

explanation.surface: A dissolute painter runs into a scoundrel while on holiday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On vacation' reads as on holiday, but it empties the word.
explanation.definitionFit: A rake is a dissolute, pleasure-seeking man, so the noun degenerate fits as a description of such a person.

clue.text: Wind up European man of wisdom

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up reads from bottom to top

blocks.note: E is the abbreviation for European

explanation.surface: Annoying a wise European thinker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wind up' reads as tease, but it is GAS turned upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A sage is a person revered for profound knowledge and good judgement, a wise elder or philosopher.

clue.text: Island nation taking part in assault on Gallipoli

indicators.note: taking part means being only a portion of the whole

explanation.surface: A Pacific country joins the First World War landings at Gallipoli.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Taking part in' sounds like military participation, but it points to letters inside the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Tonga is a Polynesian kingdom made up of many islands in the South Pacific Ocean.

clue.text: Armenia's foremost priest brings up Judges

indicators.note: the foremost part is the front, so the first letter

blocks.note: to bring up a child is to raise it

explanation.surface: Armenia's leading cleric raises a point about the Book of Judges.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Judges' looks like the Old Testament book, but it is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To appraise is to assess or evaluate something's worth, which is a way of forming a judgement on it.

clue.text: Complaint clergyman withdraws following oddly heady offer

indicators.note: the odd positions in a word are the first, third, fifth and so on
coming after something places it later in the line
to withdraw is to draw back, so it reads backwards

explanation.surface: A vicar backs out after an intoxicating proposal and makes a complaint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Complaint' reads as a grievance, but here it is an ailment.
explanation.definitionFit: A complaint can be an illness, and hay fever is an allergy to pollen causing sneezing and streaming eyes.

clue.text: Binge drink around centre of London

indicators.note: the centre of a word is its middle letters
to go around something is to enclose it

explanation.surface: A boozy night out drinking around central London.
explanation.walkthrough: BEER holds ND in its middle.
explanation.definitionFit: Bender is informal slang for a prolonged bout of heavy drinking, the same thing as a binge.
